summary: Discusses issues that arise when deploying IPv6 in mobile networks, since smartphones are speeding up IPv4 address exhaustion. It is a reference for service providers and network designers. It was replaced by RFC 6342.

eli5.summary: Phones are using up the old internet addresses fast, so the new kind is needed. This guide helps phone companies plan the switch. Replaced by RFC 6342.

questions: centralized vs distributed nat in mobile networks
why do mobile networks need nat44
subtitle: What mobile operators face when they bring IPv6 into 3G and 4G networks while IPv4 addresses run out.

tldr.problem: Mobile Internet use is speeding up the exhaustion of IPv4 addresses, and mobile networks have particular constraints (gateways, billing, roaming) that make the move to IPv6 harder.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes no new protocol. It surveys four areas: address exhaustion, where to place NAT, IPv6-only deployment and fixed-mobile convergence, and says how existing IPv6 deployment tools apply.
tldr.outcome: It is a reference for service providers and network designers. It has been obsoleted by RFC 6342.

facts.label: Reference architecture nodes
facts.value: BS, ANG, MNG, BR, AAA, PCRF

today: RFC 6312 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 6342, which is the version to read now.

sections.title: Why Mobile Networks Need IPv6
sections.content:
The RFC starts from one claim: the growth of the Mobile Internet is accelerating the exhaustion of IPv4 addresses, and IPv6 is widely accepted as necessary for the Internet to keep operating and growing. It does not propose any new protocols. It describes the challenges and where existing IPv6 deployment solutions apply.

It assumes the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) 3G and 4G architectures for the most part, and says the considerations are general enough for other mobile architectures. The IANA has exhausted the available /8 blocks for allocation to the Regional Internet Registries, so providers pursue two approaches at once: delaying IPv4 exhaustion and introducing IPv6.

Delaying exhaustion means giving end users private IPv4 addresses behind a provider-side Network Address Translator (NAT), or extending an address with port ranges. The RFC concentrates on translation: NAT44 (public IPv4 to private IPv4) and NAT64 (public IPv6 to public IPv4). It also notes that LTE needs an always-on connection to carry Voice over IP, so making that connection IPv6 saves private IPv4 addresses.
sections.eli5: There are not enough old-style addresses for all the phones. Phone companies can stretch what they have by sharing, and start using the new kind at the same time.

sections.title: The Mobile Network Reference Architecture
sections.content:
A Mobile Node (MN) reaches the network through its Home Network or, when roaming, a Visited Network. In 3GPP an MN connects to an Access Point Name (APN), which maps to a mobile gateway and says which IP connectivity (IPv4, IPv6, IPv4v6) is enabled. The end-to-end link is an Evolved Packet System (EPS) bearer in LTE or a Packet Data Protocol (PDP) context in 3G UMTS.

The nodes along the link are the Base Station, the Access Network Gateway (ANG), the Mobile Network Gateway (MNG) and the Border Router (BR). The MNG is the MN's default router and handles IP address management, Quality of Service, policy, billing and accounting, which the RFC calls subscriber management. The BR borders the Internet and does no subscriber management. AAA and the Policy and Charging Rule Function (PCRF) support authentication, billing and policy.
sections.eli5: A phone's data trip goes through several stations. One of them, the gateway, hands out addresses and keeps the bill, and another sits at the edge of the Internet.

sections.title: Where to Put the NAT
sections.content:
The private 10.0.0.0 block (NET10) has about 16.7 million addresses, and a large mobile network can have more subscribers than that at once. So where NAT44 sits matters. NAT also creates bindings that billing, accounting and policy need to correlate, and there may be legal requirements to store them.

In the centralized model a common node such as the BR manages the pool for several MNGs. Addresses then overlap, so tunnels (GRE, MPLS VPN or IP-in-IP) are needed to tell sessions apart. The drawbacks listed include extra protocols to correlate NAT state, suboptimal MN-to-MN communication and a single point of failure.

In the distributed model each MNG assigns private addresses and runs the NAT, so each can reuse the whole NET10 block. NAT state sits next to subscriber management and the AAA and PCRF interfaces. The cost is no centralized addressing or NAT management. A hybrid puts NAT in a dedicated device. The RFC says providers wanting easy integration may find the distributed model compelling, and those wanting common NAT management may prefer the centralized one.
sections.eli5: Sharing a limited set of house numbers can be done by one big post office or by many small ones. Small ones keep better track of who is who, and one big one is easier to run.

sections.title: IPv6-Only Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC treats NAT as an interim solution. It describes three dimensions of an IPv6-only move: the network, the mobile nodes and the applications. The classic dual-stack path keeps all three supporting both IPv4 and IPv6. Another path makes the network and the MN IPv6-only while applications remain mostly IPv4, which needs IPv6-IPv4 translation and DNS64 (RFC 6147). Translation is covered by RFC 6146 and RFC 6145.

Challenges include applications that are not IPv6-capable, IPv4 literals in protocols such as XMPP or in HTML and XML content, and Voice over LTE (VoLTE), where signaling is generally free while the call is charged by duration. Roaming is the biggest constraint: an IPv6-only operator must still support IPv4 connectivity and NAT44 for its outbound roamers visiting networks without IPv6 and for inbound roamers whose devices lack IPv6.

The conclusion is that IPv6-only deployments should be encouraged alongside the recommended dual-stack model, phased in for newer mobile nodes.
sections.eli5: Going fully new-style is easy for a company's own services but hard when phones travel to places that still use the old style, so the old way has to keep working for a while.

sections.title: Fixed-Mobile Convergence
sections.content:
Many providers run both fixed broadband and mobile networks. The RFC finds convergence difficult because the networks differ: fixed networks have no roaming, are not required to provide voice, and their links can usually carry both IPv6 and IPv4, unlike some mobile PDP/PDN connections.

Both still face IPv4 address management, but the solutions differ. Tunneling private IPv4 inside IPv6 works at a cable or DSL modem but not where the endpoint is the MN. The 6rd mechanism (RFC 5969) suits residential gateways, while a mobile operator can reuse its existing tunneling. Femto base stations behind a NAT may suffer from periodic cleanup of NAT state.

The RFC concludes that the provider's core network is the place where most convergence is feasible, with some harmonization also possible in services and applications.
sections.eli5: A company that runs both home internet and phone internet would like to run them the same way, but they work differently, so they mostly meet in the middle, at the core.

sections.title: Summary and Security
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes four points. Conserving IPv4 means NAT in mobile networks, and the IETF dual-stack model of RFC 4213 applies readily. Both centralized and distributed NAT placement have merits. IPv6-only deployment is feasible in LTE for an operator's own services, but roaming and older devices still need IPv4. Convergence is best at the core.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence: the document does not introduce any new security vulnerabilities.
sections.eli5: In short: share old addresses carefully, start using new ones where you can, keep the old ones working for travelers, and the core is where home and phone networks can be joined.
